WTF Is a Loop? And How to Build One This Week

Steinberger says stop prompting your agents and start designing loops that prompt them. The replies turned into a brawl over what that means. The answer is simple, it has a five-year lineage, and you can run your first loop in one line today. Here is the practical version, with the commands.

A six-word sentence had the AI-coding timeline in a chokehold this week. Peter Steinberger posted it, it cleared two million views, and the replies became a fight over what it actually meant.

"You shouldn't be prompting coding agents anymore. You should be designing loops that prompt your agents."

@steipete, June 2026

Someone asked the only useful question, what does this look like in practice, and the most-quoted reply was "nobody knows but him and boris." That is funny and it is wrong. Plenty of people know, the answer is not mystical, and the on-ramp is a single command. So instead of another think-piece about whether prompt engineering is dead, here is how to actually build one, starting from a line you can paste in the next five minutes.

Three things to take away:

  • A loop is a small program that prompts the agent for you, reads what it produced, decides whether it is done, and if not, prompts it again. You stop being the thing inside the loop typing prompts. You write the loop, and the model becomes a subroutine.
  • The simplest useful loop is one line of bash. The most useful one is a single slash command. You do not need an orchestration framework to start, and you should not begin with one.
  • Two things separate a loop that works from a loop that bankrupts you: a way for it to check its own work against an external truth, and hard stops so it halts. Everything practical in this article is about those two.

The plain definition, and the ladder

Boris Cherny built Claude Code and now reports that in a recent month, 100% of his contributions to it were written by Claude Code, 259 pull requests, with his IDE deleted since November. His description of how is the cleanest you will find: "I don't prompt Claude anymore. I have loops that are running. They're the ones prompting Claude and figuring out what to do. My job is to write loops."

Put yourself on his three-rung ladder and the idea stops being abstract. A year ago you wrote code by hand with autocomplete. Then you ran several agent sessions in parallel and prompted each one. Now you write the program that prompts the agent, and you go do something else. The job moved up an altitude, from writing the code to writing the thing that writes the code. He is clear that this does not make engineers obsolete, someone still has to decide what to build, and he argues good engineers matter more, not less. The keystrokes left. The judgment stayed.

Now the practical part.

The simplest loop: one line of bash

The whole concept fits in a bash one-liner, and it is worth running once just to feel it. This is the "ralph loop," named after Ralph Wiggum and popularized by Geoffrey Huntley in 2025:

while :; do cat PROMPT.md | claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions; done

That is the entire thing. It pipes the same prompt file into Claude Code in headless mode, lets the agent work until it exits, then starts it again with the same prompt. Each pass is a fresh session, so the agent does not remember the last one. It reorients by reading the files, the checklist, and the commits the previous pass left behind. There is no orchestration, no framework, no state machine. It is a while-true around a coding agent.

One caution before you paste it. --dangerously-skip-permissions does exactly what it says, the agent runs commands without stopping to ask. Run this in a throwaway git worktree or a container, on a branch you are willing to see rewritten, never on your main checkout.

The non-obvious trick is the discipline, not the code. Each iteration resets the context to a fixed set of anchor files instead of letting one giant conversation grow and rot. Your PROMPT.md points the agent at the same handful of files every time, usually a spec and a checklist it ticks off and commits as it goes, so the next pass starts fresh but oriented. That reset, plus committing progress each pass, is why it does not drift and does not redo finished work.

Does this trivial thing work? At a Y Combinator hackathon, a team shipped six repositories overnight on a ralph loop for about 297 dollars in API costs, work they estimated at fifty thousand dollars of contractor time. Huntley built an entire small programming language this way. The one-liner is a toy you can outgrow, but it teaches the shape of the whole idea in thirty seconds.

The catch, and the reason it is "old hat" to the people deepest in this: the ralph loop assumes your terminal stays open and never checks whether it is actually done. It just runs forever. That is the problem the next two sections solve.

The one-command version: /goal and /loop

You do not have to hand-roll the bash. Claude Code shipped two commands that are the productized, safer version of the same loop.

/goal runs the agent until a condition you state becomes true. The condition is the whole craft:

/goal all tests in test/auth pass and the lint step is clean,
      or stop after 20 turns

Here is the part that makes it more than a while-true. After each turn, Claude Code sends your condition and the conversation so far to a separate small, fast model, Haiku by default, which returns a plain yes or no and a reason. A "no" feeds that reason back as guidance for the next turn. The model that does the work is not the model that decides it is done.

One catch matters more than any other here: that judge does not run your tests or read your repo. It only reads what already landed in the transcript. So the condition has to be something the agent's own output can prove. "All tests in test/auth pass" works because the agent runs the tests and the result is sitting right there in the conversation for the judge to read. "The auth is solid" does not, because nothing in the transcript settles it. You are not asking the judge to verify your code, you are asking it to read the receipts the agent already produced. Which means the real verification is still the agent running a real command. The judge just decides whether the receipt says pass.

A good condition has two parts: one measurable end state, and a stated way the agent proves it in its output. "Make the auth better" is not a condition. "All tests in test/auth pass, npm test exits 0, and git status shows only the auth files changed" is, because every clause shows up in the transcript as something the agent ran. Always add a cap, "or stop after 20 turns," and pass --max-turns 20 as a hard backstop, so an unattended run cannot grind forever.

Run unattended in one shot with claude -p --max-turns 20 "/goal ...". The process has to stay alive while it works, so this is a terminal you leave open or a server, not a closed laptop. If you genuinely want to shut the lid, that is what Claude Code in the cloud is for. Ctrl+C stops a local run early.

In practice a short run looks like this, two turns and about forty cents:

> /goal all tests in test/auth pass, npm test exits 0, or stop after 15 turns

◎ /goal active · turn 1
  ran: npm test
  ✗ 2 failing in test/auth/login.test.ts
  judge: not done, expired-token case still throws

◎ /goal active · turn 2
  edited src/auth/token.ts
  ran: npm test
  ✓ 41 passing, exit 0
  judge: done, npm test exits 0 and only auth files changed

✓ goal achieved · 2 turns · ~$0.40

That is the whole mechanism on screen: the agent runs the check, the result lands in the transcript, the judge reads it and says keep going or stop.

/loop is the scheduled, babysitting cousin. Boris's own starter example is the one to copy and change the nouns on:

/loop babysit all my PRs. Auto-fix build issues, and when
      comments come in, use a worktree agent to fix them.

That re-runs on a time interval, picks up whatever is new since the last pass, and keeps going until you stop it or it decides the work is done. It is polling, not magic event handling, but for "watch my PRs and fix what breaks" polling is exactly enough. You wrote the intent and the stopping behavior, not the steps. Then a few days later Boris posted his recipe for running an agent autonomously for hours or days, and the last tip is the one that matters most.

The part that makes it trustworthy: self-verification

An open loop that writes code and never checks it is a machine for generating confident mistakes, faster and faster. So the loop has to verify its own work against something external and objective, not against its own opinion.

The rule the practitioners converge on: external verification decides when the task is complete, not the model's self-assessment. The loop keeps going not when the agent says "this looks good," but when docker build succeeds, the container starts, and the health check passes. Objective criteria, not vibes. A loop body that actually holds up looks like this in pseudocode:

loop:
  agent: make progress on the task
  run:   npm test  (or the build, or the linter)
  if check passes:   done, exit
  if check fails:    feed the failure back, try again
  if no progress in N tries, or budget hit: stop and ping me

Two refinements that the people running this in production swear by. First, use a different model to review than the one that wrote the code, because the same model carries the same blind spots, so a fresh reviewer catches what the author cannot. Dan Kornas built a tool called roborev that reviews every commit in the background and feeds the findings back to the agent while the context is still fresh, which is this pattern as a product. Second, run at least two review passes even when the first finds nothing, and hard-cap at five or six rounds so it cannot oscillate forever.

The loop is not the magic. The feedback inside it is. A loop with a real check is an engine, a loop without one is just a billing event.

The part that keeps you solvent: guardrails

Once the model writes the code for almost nothing, the cost moves to the loop running it, and an unbounded loop is a genuine financial hazard. Uber capped its engineers at 1,500 dollars per person per tool per month for Claude Code and Cursor after burning its annual AI budget in four months. The failure everyone in production fears is the loop that does not stop, the one that turns a forgotten terminal into a four-figure invoice overnight.

Every serious loop has the same three hard stops, and you should add all three before you ever leave one running unattended:

max_iterations:   stop after N turns           (the runaway cap)
no_progress:      stop if M turns change nothing (the stuck cap)
budget_ceiling:   stop at $X or T tokens         (the wallet cap)
on_stop:          ping me with the state and the reason

/goal gives you the runaway cap almost for free: put "or stop after 20 turns" in the condition and pass --max-turns 20. The other two you add yourself. The no-progress detector is not automatic, the simplest version is a Stop hook or a small wrapper that compares git diff --stat between turns and halts when nothing has changed for a few rounds. The budget ceiling lives in your provider's spend controls, a hard dollar limit on the workspace you set once in the Console before you ever leave a loop running. The romantic pitch for loops is that you write them and a thousand agents build your company overnight. The production reality is that you write them, and most of the engineering is making sure they halt.

The asset inside the loop is a skill, not a prompt

Here is where I land after building these. The loop is plumbing. The valuable thing is what it calls.

Steinberger's other recurring point is the durable half of his advice: if you do something more than once, turn it into a reusable skill, and if you do something hard, turn it into a skill afterward so next time is free. A loop that re-derives how to run your tests, find your config, and format your output on every single iteration is paying the model to relearn your project forever. A loop that calls a small library of named, tested skills, "run the suite," "open a PR the way we open PRs," "deploy to staging," compounds, because each iteration starts from competence instead of from scratch. It is cheaper and it does not drift. The skills are the asset. The loop is just the thing that calls them in order.

Where it goes: loops supervising loops

The frontier, and what Steinberger and Boris actually mean by the new thing, is loops that supervise other loops. One loop dispatches work to several agents at once, watches them, and decides what runs next, with durable git-backed state so the whole thing survives a crash. Steve Yegge's open-source Gas Town is the vivid example: twenty to thirty Claude Code instances coordinated by a "Mayor" agent, with patrol agents running continuous loops. Claude Code's own dynamic workflows are the productized version, where the agent writes the orchestration script and runs a fleet of subagents for you.

You do not start here. You start with one /goal, add a self-verify, add the three caps, and only reach for orchestration when a single loop genuinely cannot hold the work. Most people need that later than the hype suggests.

Build your first loop this week

A concrete plan, nothing exotic.

  1. Start on a throwaway branch and prove your check by hand. git checkout -b loop-test, then run your test command once yourself and confirm it exits non-zero when something is broken. If the agent cannot tell pass from fail, neither can the judge.
  2. Pick one bounded task with an objective done. A flaky test, a small migration, a lint cleanup. Nothing where "finished" is a matter of taste.
  3. Write it as a /goal with a cap. A real command, not a shape: claude --max-turns 15 "/goal all tests in test/auth pass, npm test exits 0, or stop after 15 turns".
  4. Confirm the agent can run the check end to end. Deps installed, no interactive prompt waiting for a keypress, the command exits non-zero on failure. This is where first runs silently stall.
  5. Run it and watch the first one. Do not walk away. Watch where the judge says "not done" and what the agent does when a check fails. Ctrl+C kills it.
  6. Cap the spend before you run one unattended. Set a hard dollar limit on the workspace in the Console, and keep --max-turns on every run. The turn cap stops a runaway, the dollar cap stops a slow bleed.
  7. Save the repeated part as a skill. The test command, your PR steps, the thing you found yourself re-explaining. Drop it in a SKILL.md so the next loop starts from competence instead of re-deriving it.

By the end of the week you will have shipped real work you did not type, watched it check and correct itself, and capped it so it cannot run off a cliff. That is the entire practice in miniature.

The answer to "what is a loop" is not a take about prompt engineering dying. It is this: stop being the thing in the loop. Write the loop once, give it a real check and reusable skills, cap it so it halts, and let it run while you go decide what to build next. Steinberger and Boris are describing the same animal from two sides. The good news is that, as of this month, the front door is a single slash command.
